tagline.text: A city of love flowing between batchoy and old mansions

children.text: The central city of Panay Island, which flourished on the Spanish-era sugar trade. It's a great food-and-walking city in the Visayas, where you can stroll and eat your way through the old shopping street Calle Real, the riverside Esplanade, historic churches, and La Paz batchoy.

Iloilo City is the central city of the Western Visayas region, in the southeast of Panay Island facing the Guimaras Strait. It flourished as a sugar and textile trading port during the Spanish colonial era in the 19th century, ranking as the richest city after Manila, and in

it received the title "La Muy Leal y Noble Ciudad" (the Most Loyal and Noble City) from the Spanish crown. Stone mansions and shop buildings built by sugar barons of that era, along with beautiful churches, still stand throughout the city today.

The city is divided into districts based on its old town units — City Proper, Molo, Jaro, La Paz, Mandurriao, Arevalo, Lapuz, and others. Each district has its own plaza, church, and signature dish, making it fun to explore the city district by district. More recently, a large mixed-use development has risen on the site of the old airport in Mandurriao district, giving the city a modern skyline.

The people of Iloilo, known as Ilonggos, are famous for their soft, gentle way of speaking, which has earned the city the nickname "City of Love." It's often cited as one of the most liveable cities in the Philippines thanks to its cleanliness and well-developed bike lanes and riverside paths, and it gets high marks among Korean expats and long-term residents too.

It suits travellers who enjoy walking, eating, and sightseeing over flashy tourist attractions, and those interested in historic architecture and churches. It's also a good starting point for a West Visayas trip that continues on to Guimaras, Miagao, Islas de Gigantes, and Bacolod.
A rich noodle soup topped with pork offal, liver, and crispy pork cracklings, La Paz batchoy is Iloilo's signature dish. You can try a bowl for about
at one of the old batchoy stalls inside La Paz Market.

An old commercial district centered on J.M. Basa Street, lined with restored early-20th-century neoclassical and art deco shophouses. It's especially nice to walk here at dusk when the lights come on.

A Gothic Revival church built of coral stone, nicknamed the "feminist church" because the statues lining its interior columns depict only female saints. Try pancit Molo, a clear dumpling soup, nearby.
A cathedral dedicated to Our Lady of Candelaria, notable for its bell tower standing separately in the plaza across the street. A major celebration is held here every
February 2
for the Feast of Candelaria.
A riverside promenade stretching for several kilometers, where mangroves meet city views. It's a favourite spot for an early morning jog or an evening stroll.

blocks.title: See the old mansions of Jaro

children.text: Mansions built by sugar barons, such as Nelly's Garden, are clustered in Jaro district. Most are private property, so it's best to admire them from the outside, but check whether there are open events or pre-booked tours.
A 19th-century stone mansion in Arevalo district, now a living museum where you can experience the daily life and traditional food of an old Ilonggo household. Booking ahead may be required.
A Santo Niño festival held around the fourth weekend of
January
each year, when dance troupes in tribal costume fill the whole city with a dynamic parade.
Batchoy for breakfast at La Paz Market, followed by local coffee at a nearby old café

Buy snacks like biscocho at an old bakery in Jaro
Molo Church and Molo Plaza, a late lunch of pancit Molo
Stroll Calle Real heritage street, visit a museum

1 hour 10 minutes

from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), with several daily flights on Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and AirAsia. There are also direct flights from Cebu, Davao, Cagayan de Oro, and elsewhere.
The airport is in Cabatuan, about
19km
from downtown. The airport shuttle van (to city malls) costs about
per person, while a taxi or Grab costs about
, with a travel time of
30–45 minutes
A fast craft from Bacolod takes about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
and costs about
per person (depending on seat class). OceanJet, Weesam Express, and others run several times a day.
Large passenger ferries also sail from Manila, but the trip takes over
20 hours
, so flying is the more practical option for most travellers.
From Boracay (Caticlan) to Iloilo takes about
5–6 hours
by bus, with an air-conditioned bus costing about
per person. Buses and vans also run frequently from Kalibo and Roxas.
Jeepneys are the cheapest way to get around town (base fare about
), and Grab and taxis are easy to find. Taxi rides between districts usually cost
The dry season, from
December
to
May
, is best for exploring the city on foot.
December–February
is relatively cool, while March to
May
is hot, so it's better to plan activities for the morning and evening rather than midday. From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent showers, but few days see rain all day long, so city sightseeing is still quite feasible. Typhoons mainly affect the area between August and
November
During the Dinagyang Festival, around the fourth weekend of
January
, accommodation books up months in advance and roads are closed, so book early if you want to see the festival, or avoid this period otherwise. The Jaro Candelaria Festival on
February 2
and Holy Week events in
April
are also worth seeing.

Accommodation splits broadly into two areas. The City Proper area near Calle Real and the river is great for walking and soaking up the old-town atmosphere, while the new downtown in Mandurriao district is convenient, with large malls, chain hotels, and a restaurant strip. Mid-range hotels run about
a night, business hotels
and up, and there are also many Airbnb-style condos.

Iloilo is one of the top food cities in the Philippines. Beyond La Paz batchoy, signature dishes include pancit Molo, a clear dumpling soup with shrimp and pork meatballs, crisp-baked treats like biscocho and butter cookies, and old-bakery snacks from Jaro district. Madge Café, which has operated inside La Paz Market since the
, is a traditional coffee shop beloved by locals, and the coastal Arevalo district is home to a cluster of seafood restaurants. Chicken inasal here is every bit as good as in Bacolod.
Churches and old mansions photograph best, and are less hot to visit, early in the morning or after
When visiting church interiors, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and avoid taking photos during Mass.
Many batchoy stalls open early in the morning and stay open late, making it a good breakfast option.
It's also nice to rent a bike and ride the length of the Esplanade. The city government has steadily expanded its bike lanes.
Grab is easy to find, but waiting times get longer during the rainy evening rush hour (
5–7 PM
), so allow extra time.
For souvenirs, a regional specialty shop inside a mall or a bakery in Jaro is a safe bet for biscocho, dried mango, and piaya pastries.
If you plan a day trip to Guimaras, leave from Parola wharf early in the morning to have enough time to look around properly.
The National Museum Western Visayas Regional Museum, housed in the former provincial jail building, and the Museum of Philippine Economic History are free, Museo Iloilo costs about
, and the Iloilo Museum of Contemporary Art (ILOMOCA) costs about
. Check in advance the days the National Museum is closed and how entry reservations work.
The city is relatively safe, but watch out for pickpockets in crowded places like markets and terminals, and don't keep your phone in your back pocket.

Crowds during the Dinagyang Festival are enormous, so carry only minimal valuables and agree on a meeting point with your group in advance. Parade viewing areas are often run as paid seating, so check ahead.
Some roads can flood during the rainy season, so check the weather before heading into low-lying areas.
Many of the old mansions are private property. Don't climb over fences or enter without permission.
